1:
Whether the opening verse looks back or forward is settled twice and unsettled once. John Calvin calls it unnatural and forced to suppose with some expositors that this is a prediction of what was to come, says he has no doubt the psalm was composed upon the return itself, and translates the verb in the past tense accordingly. Keil and Delitzsch agree and are harsher, granting that some transfer the grateful retrospect into the future, but holding the reasons for it silenced by the requirements of the syntax. John Gill takes exactly the position they condemn: though it is expressed in the past tense, it may be put for the future and considered as a prophecy, and he renders the following verse as then shall our mouth be filled with laughter, adding that a Jewish commentary refers the whole to the world to come. On the author, Adam Clarke observes the psalm has no title in the Hebrew or any of the versions and belongs certainly to the close of the captivity, reporting two guesses at its composer; the paragraph attached to Calvin’s block names another pair of scholars making the second of the same guesses.

The word rendered dream is disputed, and one of the disputed readings turns out to be the one an early expositor was working from. Charles Ellicott notes that the two oldest versions have as if consoled, and that the Hebrew word means primarily to be fat or fleshy and is elsewhere rendered recover, a sense the Aramaic paraphrases adopt with we were like men who have recovered. Augustine of Hippo has precisely that first alternative in his text and expounds it: we became as those that are comforted, by which he means we became joyful. The others keep dreaming, and two of them independently reach for the same ancient parallel to illustrate it. Clarke tells at length how the Romans, having vanquished the Macedonian king, proclaimed liberty to the Greek cities by a herald at the games, and says the tidings produced nearly the same effect on that assembly as the decree of release did upon the Jews. Ellicott cites the same historian’s account of the same occasion, and his quotation supplies the very figure of the psalm: the joy was too great for men to take in, none could believe he had heard aright, and they looked on one another in wonder, like the empty show of a dream.

Matthew Henry supplies the psalm’s emotional history from the psalm before it, that the harps had been hung on the willow-trees while God called to weeping, and are now resumed, since Providence pipes to them and they dance; and he adds that harps are never more melodiously tunable than after such a melancholy disuse, the long want of mercies greatly sweetening their return. He also states the purpose of the captivity in one figure, that they were sent into it not as dross is put into the fire to be consumed but as gold to be refined. On the third verse Gill makes an unusual re-assignment: the words are generally supposed to be those of the Jews taking up what the heathen had said, but he sees no reason why they should not be the heathen speaking still, declaring that the great things done were not for that people only but for themselves also. Clarke keeps them for the returned exiles and calls the last clause a mere burst of ecstatic joy. John Wesley fixes simply on the astonishment, and C.H. Spurgeon quotes a couplet asking that if this be a dream the sleeper not be woken yet. Augustine asks instead how the captivity began, and answers that we sold ourselves by consenting to the seducer, and could sell ourselves but could not redeem ourselves.
4:
Who is prayed for in the fourth verse is answered four ways. John Gill observes that the petition shows the captivity was not yet over, but reports that some take it as the prayer of those already home for the brethren who stayed behind, enjoying the sweets of their liberty and asking that others come and share them; his own preference runs further forward, either to the coming of the Redeemer or to the conversion of that people in a later day. Matthew Henry keeps it historical and doubles it, since those who had returned were still in distress in their own land while many yet remained abroad, so that they rejoiced with trembling. Adam Clarke allows that it may be a recital of the prayer used before the deliverance, or else a petition for those still in the far provinces, noting that the captives did not all come back at once but at different times and under different leaders. Charles Ellicott takes the simplest of these, that the poet now thinks of the many still dispersed among the nations. Henry draws the rule from it, that the beginnings of mercy are encouragements to pray for its completion, and that while we are in this world there will still be matter for prayer even when we are best furnished with matter for praise.

The comparison attached to that prayer divides Clarke from everyone else. He suspects a great river, arguing that the one he names rises far in the south and runs northward through several countries before dividing and emptying into the sea, though he allows that some other rapid southward rivers might be meant, and that what is asked is a return as rapid and abundant as their waters. Ellicott corrects the picture: the word means channels rather than streams, and the allusion is to the sudden filling of the dry torrent-beds of the southern district in the rainy season, so that the prayer is for torrents of returning people to pour into a deserted country. John Wesley and Henry both take it the same way, of floods sent into dry and parched southern ground, and Keil and Delitzsch likewise have the land thirsting as the southern country toward the desert thirsts. Ellicott adds that the Greek version read a south wind here and evidently imagined the melting of a frozen stream rather than the filling of a dry bed.

On the proverb that closes the psalm, two of them suspect it was not coined for the occasion. Clarke says it is either a maxim gathered from their own history or a fact they are now witnessing. Ellicott goes further and says something finer: the poet probably found the saying already current, but has touched it with the consecrating hand until it has become only less precious than a saying of divine lips about those who mourn being comforted. Ellicott also prefers singing to joy in the same verse, and contrasts the harvest-home songs with the anxiety of the seed-time. Gill offers two reasons why the seed is called precious, either because bought at a great price when grain is dear, or because the choicest wheat is what is kept for sowing. Clarke turns the last verse into a sustained scene: a poor farmer after a bad harvest has saved a little seed out of the famine, and must either sow it or despair; he carries it in his basket and with a sorrowful heart commits it to the furrow, watering it in effect with his tears; the season turns mild, he sees in succession the blade, the ear and the full corn, and at the appointed weeks of harvest fills his arms and his carriages with sheaves and returns in triumph to his expecting family. So, Clarke concludes, shall it be with the handful returning, who are themselves to be sown and scattered over the land.
